Trevor Story hit a three-run homer in the eighth inning as the Boston Red Sox overcame a three-run deficit to defeat the Texas Rangers 4-3 on Thursday in Arlington, Texas.
Story’s blast came against Texas closer Jacob Latz (3-3) and erased a 3-1 deficit.
The victory allowed Boston (83-70) to avoid being swept in the three-game series and ended the Rangers’ four-game winning streak. Josh Jung hit a solo home run for Texas (76-77), which fell a game behind the Houston Astros (77-76) at the top of the American League West.
Wyatt Olds (2-0) earned the win by tossing one scoreless inning. Boston starter Sonny Gray allowed three runs on three hits in 6 1/3 innings. He struck out six and walked three.
Texas had the tying run on first with one out in the ninth, but Garrett Whitlock got Jake Burger to ground into a game-ending double play for his fourth save.
Danny Jansen had two of the Rangers’ four hits, including an RBI single.
Boston’s Willson Contreras left the game after he was hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning. Contreras leads the Red Sox with 27 home runs.
Jung hit a solo shot in the first inning to open the scoring. It was his 10th homer of the season.
Texas extended its lead to 3-0 in the third. After two walks and a sacrifice bunt, Jansen singled home Wyatt Langford, and Burger scored on Evan Carter’s sacrifice bunt.
The Red Sox got on the scoreboard in the seventh. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin walked, and Eaton took third on a flyout. A throwing error by second baseman Nicky Lopez on Roman Anthony’s grounder brought in Eaton.
In the eighth, Boston’s Wilyer Abreu walked and Contreras was hit by a Jakob Junis pitch. Latz entered and got Adley Rutschman to foul out before Story belted a 2-2 curveball to left-center, handing Boston a 4-3 lead. It was Story’s fourth homer of the year.
The Boston offense struggled in the first two games of the series. The Red Sox struck out 15 times as the Rangers won 4-2 on Tuesday, and the visitors were held to three hits in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday.

ARLINGTON -- Trevor Story esperó más de cuatro meses para conectar su siguiente jonrón. Y llegó justo a tiempo para los Medias Rojas.
Story finalmente despertó con un cuadrangular de tres carreras que puso a Boston al frente en el octavo inning la noche del jueves, impulsando a los Medias Rojas a una victoria por 4-3 sobre los Rangers en el Globe Life Field y ayudándolos a evitar su primera barrida desde julio.
Wilyer Abreu abrió el octavo episodio con una base por bolas antes de que Willson Contreras fuera golpeado por un lanzamiento y saliera del juego, con Isiah Kiner-Falefa ingresando como corredor emergente. Story entonces atacó una curva de 80.3 mph y la mandó en línea entre los jardines izquierdo y central para su primer vuelacercas desde el 13 de mayo y su cuarto de la temporada.
Boston había comenzado a reducir la desventaja un capítulo antes. Después de boletos consecutivos a Caleb Durbin y Nate Eaton, Roman Anthony bateó un rodado para una jugada forzada que permitió anotar a Eaton. Un error en tiro del segunda base Nicky López en la jugada permitió que Anthony avanzara a la intermedia.
La remontada en las últimas entradas llegó después de que Sonny Gray mantuviera a los Medias Rojas a una distancia alcanzable pese a un complicado comienzo de su apertura.
El derecho de 36 años lanzó 6.1 entradas, permitiendo tres carreras y tres hits, con seis ponches y tres bases por bolas en 102 pitcheos, su mayor cantidad de la temporada, de los cuales 67 fueron strikes.

ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Trevor Story hit a three-run home run off All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning, capping a comeback from a three-run deficit as the Boston Red Sox beat Texas 4-3 on Thursday night and dropped the Rangers out of the AL West lead.
Texas (76-77) had won four straight games to gain a share of the lead but dropped one game behind Houston (77-76), which holds the tiebreaker. The Rangers trail by two games for the last AL wild card.
Boston (83-70) has a five-game lead for the top AL wild card and improved to 8-59 when trailing after seven innings. Texas dropped to 63-2 when leading after seven innings.
Latz (3-3) entered after Wilyer Abreu walked starting the eighth and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch from Jakob Junis.
Latz struck out Adley Rutschman and Story, who is from nearby Irving, reached down for Latz's second straight low curveball and drove the ball over the left-field wall for his fourth home run this season.
Boston’s Wyatt Olds (2-0) got three outs and Garrett Whitlock pitched the ninth for his fourth save in eight chances, getting Jake Burger to ground into a game-ending double play.
Josh Jung hit a first-inning homer off Sonny Gray, and Texas opened a 3-0 lead in the second on Danny Jansen's RBI single and Evan Carter's safety squeeze bunt.
Roman Anthony hit into a run-scoring forceout in the seventh.
Texas’ Cody Bradford followed a one-inning opener with 4 1/3 shutout innings, seeking his first major league since Sept. 18, 2024. He missed last season following elbow surgery.
Gray gave up three hits in 6 1/3 innings, throwing a season-high 102 pitches.

item.content:encoded:
This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

The Boston Red Sox need something to change Thursday night. Putting Jarren Duran back in the lineup is a start.
Boston will turn to Duran in center field for Thursday's series finale against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field after he did not start Wednesday's 7-3 loss. The Red Sox have dropped the first two games of the series and enter Thursday at 82-70 with only 10 games remaining in the regular season.
Roman Anthony will remain in the leadoff spot and start in left field, while Jahmai Jones gets another opportunity at designated hitter. Wilyer Abreu, Willson Contreras and Adley Rutschman make up the middle of the order.
Christopher Smith of MassLive shared Boston's lineup shortly after it was released Thursday.
The complete Red Sox lineup:
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Willson Contreras, 1B
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Trevor Story, SS
- Jarren Duran, CF
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Nick Sogard, 2B
Sonny Gray will start on the mound.
Red Sox bring Duran back for crucial series finale
Duran's return is one of the most notable changes from Wednesday's lineup. The 30-year-old was not in the starting nine Wednesday, when Boston used Nate Eaton in center field and Isiah Kiner-Falefa at second base.
Red Sox lineup: Anthony LF, Jones DH, Abreu RF, Contreras 1B, Rutschman C, Story SS, Duran LF, Durbin 3B, Sogard 2B, Gray P
— Christopher Smith (@SmittyOnMLB) September 17, 2026
Neither is starting Thursday.
Instead, Duran returns to center, Sogard takes over at second and Trevor Story moves up one spot in the order to hit sixth.
Boston could certainly use a spark.
The Red Sox entered Texas with an opportunity to strengthen their postseason position but instead have lost consecutive games to a Rangers team fighting for its own playoff life. Texas improved to 76-76 with Wednesday's victory and has won four consecutive games. The Rangers are only one game behind the Chicago White Sox for the final American League wild-card spot.
Boston remains in much better shape, holding the second AL wild card with a five-game cushion over Chicago entering Thursday. That cushion is significant. It isn't comfortable enough to keep losing.
The Red Sox have gone 5-5 over their last 10 games, and Thursday represents their final opportunity to leave Texas with something positive before the schedule moves into its final nine games.
Sonny Gray gets the ball with Red Sox needing a win
If there is a pitcher Boston would want on the mound in this situation, Gray makes a compelling case. The veteran right-hander enters Thursday with a 17-5 record and 2.76 ERA.
Texas will counter with left-hander Tyler Alexander, who enters at 5-2 with a 3.38 ERA. The left-handed starter helps explain some of Boston's lineup decisions.
Jones, a right-handed hitter, remains in the No. 2 spot after starting there Wednesday. Contreras gives Boston another right-handed bat in the cleanup position, while Rutschman follows him from the fifth spot.
Anthony remains atop everything.
Boston has continued trusting the rookie in the leadoff role during the most important stretch of the season, and that won't change with a left-hander on the mound Thursday.
The larger question is whether the Red Sox can finally turn opportunities into enough runs.
Boston's postseason position remains favorable, but the Rangers have provided a reminder of how quickly September can become uncomfortable.
A sweep would send the Red Sox into the final nine games on a three-game losing streak. A win would allow them to leave Texas with their playoff cushion intact and Gray having stopped the bleeding. With Duran back in the lineup, Boston is hoping Thursday looks considerably different from the first two nights of the series. First pitch from Globe Life Field is scheduled for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

Garett Crochet wants to pitch in the postseason without making a single rehab appearance. That’s audacious enough, but how about playing in the postseason, without having ever played in the big leagues at all? That could be the situation Braiden Ward finds himself in. If you need to refresh your memory, Ward was the little speedster who was running wild all over Grapefruit League diamonds this spring. He hasn’t gotten a chance to show whether he can do that in the Majors yet, but Chad Tracy isn’t ruling it out. “Every time he gets on, he’s not afraid,” Tracy said. “That’s the thing. If he gets on base, he’s looking to go. That’s a unique trait. There’s a lot of guys who can run and steal bases and then there’s other guys who are, every single time they get on, almost regardless of the timing.” (Conor Ryan, Boston.com)
But a lack of speed on the base paths isn’t really the Red Sox problem right now as they muddle through a middling September. Strikeouts are. “The Red Sox are swinging and missing too much and not walking enough. This month, they have the eighth-most strikeouts and seventh-fewest walks. That doesn’t play in the postseason. Making contact does.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
After he initially returned to the big leagues with a bang, Roman Anthony is one of the Sox hitters who’s struggling to make contact right now. But he doesn’t sound worried. “I’m right where I want to be,” said Anthony. “I came back with enough time to get a good number of plate appearances, and to fail like I am right now and to succeed like I did in the beginning, and then kind of meet in the middle and continue to grind out every single day and get ready for what we want to be a long postseason run. [The playoffs are] what you play for after such a long year … At the end of the day, those few weeks are the only thing that really matters.” (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
Unfortunately, the other big power threat in the Sox lineup is also struggling to get back up to speed. Willson Contreras homered last night, but he’s still dealing with a nagging hamstring injury. “I ran pretty good there on the ground ball to shortstop, but I need to manage my leg better,” he said. “I know it’s feeling good and it’s feeling alright, but on a hard-hit ball like that, I know I’m going to be out. I was just trying to put pressure on him, see if he made a bad throw or whatever. Next time, I’ll manage better.” (Chris Cotillo, MassLive)
With Anthony and Contreras struggling in different ways, it’s important to remember that this team’s success has been built on depth, not individual star power. “Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.” (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
Fortunately, the Sox have some depth in the good guy department, too. After the departure of Liam Hendriks, who had been nominated for the Clemente Award seven times throughout his career for his charitable efforts, Garrett Whitlock has stepped in and picked up the baton. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)

If there has been one player on the 2026 Boston Red Sox who has had a polarizing season, it would be speedy outfielder Jarren Duran.
This past offseason, Duran was talked about as a potential trade chip, but Boston didn't make a move. The same can be said about the 2026 trade deadline as well. Boston has stuck by Duran, despite the fact that he is in the middle of the most difficult season of his career to this point. Duran has played in 142 games for Boston this season and he is slashing .204/.260/.360 with a .621 OPS, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 19 stolen bases, 15 doubles, four triples and 65 runs scored.
Despite the fact that Duran has had a tough season, Boston has arguably made the right call by sticking with him. There are positives when it comes to Duran. Right now, he's in the 92nd percentile in baserunning run value and the 90th percentile in outs above average. It's been tough for Duran to consistently get on base, but when he has gotten on base, he's a problem for opposing clubs. Also, he's been very good defensively this season. Roman Anthony missed months of action due to injury and Duran has stepped up with potentially the best defensive season of his career. In comparison, last year Duran was in the 18th percentile in outs above average. He has shown clear growth defensively and that shouldn't be ignored.
Boston Made The Right Call
Shockingly, Duran is one homer away from tying his career high of 21. Duran is also fourth on the Red Sox in RBIs with 69. If he can steal one more base this season, he'll record just his second 20-20 season of his big league career to this point.
There's no denying the fact that Duran has had a tough season overall. Right now, his OPS+ is 74. In comparison, it was 114 last year. He has regressed offensively and has struggled to get on base. But his defense has been really good, he has been a menace on the basepaths and he has been better than most on the club when runners have been on base. With his overall struggles, his trade value was very low this summer. If Boston has dealt him, imagine where the club would be right now with both Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White both hurt?
Duran has gotten consistent opportunities all season, in large part due to the injuries. When the playoffs come, if the Red Sox's outfield is at full strength, they could easily utilize an outfield of Anthony, Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu and someone else as the club's designated hitter, like Mickey Gasper. Even if Duran isn't a consistent piece in the playoff lineup, Boston could use his elite speed as a pinch runner.
Duran's season hasn't been up to his standards, but he has still helped the 2026 Red Sox overall and there's still time for more. If the Red Sox had flipped him for some sort of minor league project because his value was low, that likely wouldn't have helped the club down the stretch. Duran still can and then in the offseason Boston can figure out next steps.

If you wanted an early preview of what playoff baseball will look like for the Boston Red Sox in 2026, Wednesday night was that exact setup.
The Texas Rangers are fighting for their playoff lives, while the Red Sox have the luxury of having their wild-card spot all but assured. That meant Texas threw the best pitchers they could from start to finish, with MacKenzie Gore handing off to Jakob Junis in the middle innings before ex-Red Sox Nathan Eovaldi piggybacked the final four innings.
Well, the Red Sox only had three hits on the night in a disappointing 7-3 loss, and it highlighted a larger problem. Too many of this team's key offensive contributors are sleepwalking through September, with young star outfielder Roman Anthony topping the short list. Let's break down the three primary culprits.
1. Roman Anthony
Anthony came off the injured list guns blazing at first, but the last 11 games have been a grind. He's 7-for-49 (.149 AVG) with a .429 OPS and just one extra-base hit in those last 51 plate appearances. He's not taking his walks, he's not hitting for power, and he looks caught in between on far too many swings.
Too much of this offense was built to run through Anthony, which is evident as much when he's struggling as it was when he was injured. But if Willson Contreras isn't going to homer every night, then Anthony has to be ready to provide a big swing in October. This is where it would have really helped for him to have gotten some playoff experience last year.
2. Adley Rutschman
You can be certain that when the Red Sox gave up five pieces for Rutschman , including three of their top five prospects, they expected more than a .609 OPS and 0.1 bWAR in the first 24 games. But the trade was made to have a locked-in starting catcher for October who could add thump to the lineup, so all could soon be forgiven.
Rutschman just isn't making enough quality contact, and one can almost see him pressing to make up for the slow start that was exacerbated by wrist and elbow injuries. It's easy to tell a guy he needs to find more barrels, but a lot harder to find the advice that gets him to do it.
3. Wilyer Abreu
Abreu is having one of the quietest 6-WAR seasons in recent memory, and it's not as if the Red Sox should be demanding more from him, all things considered. That said, for this team to make a deep playoff run, the notoriously streaky lefty is going to have to get hot.
While Abreu can carry a team when he's seeing the ball well, his propensity for hitless games is worth tracking. He's got five of them already in September, including the last two in a row, and while he's been better in the second half than the first, his last few games have looked shaky.

ARLINGTON, Texas — In his long-awaited return to the Red Sox lineup, Roman Anthony has offered two very different glimpses.
In his first five games, he launched line-to-line rockets while going 10 for 22, five of those hits for extra bases, with a .455/.500/.909 slash line.
Over the next 11 games — including Wednesday’s 7-3 loss at the Rangers when he went 0 for 3 with a walk and a strikeout — he’s hit .149/.216/.213 with 18 strikeouts in 51 plate appearances (35 percent strikeout rate).
So how does the 22-year-old view his performance?
“I’m right where I want to be,” said Anthony.
While Anthony is unhappy with the strikeouts, his swing decisions — attacking strikes, limiting chases — have been close to his norms. He’s swung and missed more than usual (particularly when chasing pitches), but sees that as correctable.
More significantly, as much as Anthony wants to produce, he also appreciates the full arc of his return.
He is checking boxes — the reassurance that he can go on a tear to spearhead the Sox lineup, the need to find his way out of a slump — to regain a normal rhythm in time for the most important stage of the season.
“I came back with enough time to get a good number of plate appearances, and to fail like I am right now and to succeed like I did in the beginning, and then kind of meet in the middle and continue to grind out every single day and get ready for what we want to be a long postseason run,” he said. “[The playoffs are] what you play for after such a long year. … At the end of the day, those few weeks are the only thing that really matters.”
For Anthony, the prospect of the playoffs looms as the ultimate carrot in a tumultuous year. As a rookie in 2025, he offered a dazzling display of talent in the regular season but was reduced to the role of spectating from Fort Myers while rehabbing his oblique strain as the Sox were knocked out of the playoffs by the Yankees in the Wild Card series.
This year, he concluded a stint of nearly four months on the IL due to a partially torn ligament at the base of his right ring finger just in time to get out of Fort Myers and join the Sox in the late stages of their push towards — and, he hopes, deep into — October.
“When you’re part of a team and watching from a distance, it sucks,” said Anthony. “I looked back at last year a lot in the offseason and was like, ‘Man, I wish I was there,’ and just thought of the different scenarios of what could have potentially happened if I was there.
“[That experience] just kind of motivated me to get back there,” he added. “Obviously this year has been a roller coaster. Getting back now and being healthy right now is about getting back there and making sure that I can get that opportunity [to play in the playoffs] this time around.”
For Anthony, the idea of taking part in the playoffs comes with an exciting element of the unknown. And yet he also appreciates that, despite missing last year’s postseason, he has had an experience to prime him for games of immense consequence.
This past March, Anthony experienced the electricity of the World Baseball Classic. He was a game-changer, hitting .280/.400/.520 with two homers and seven RBIs in seven games — a run that included a go-ahead homer to propel Team USA past the Dominican Republic in the semifinals.
Yet that experience, too, left a bit of a bitter aftertaste. In the WBC Final against Venezuela, Anthony struck out for the last out of a 3-2 loss in the championship game.
“[It] went from 100 to zero because I felt like I had done so well and contributed so well … to then, as a person who is hard on himself, being like, ‘Oh man, I should have put the ball in play. I should have done something there,’ ” he reflected.
“That one stung for a little while and took me a little while to kind of work through. You ask any competitor, anytime something ends other than in a win or holding that trophy up, it’s a failure.
“It was a great experience for me. Obviously, that was a sore way to go out. But I learned what that felt like and let it sit with me for a little bit. I was able to work through it and learn [how to handle it] at a young age,” he said. “I haven’t really experienced the other end of that feeling yet.”
Anthony is now chasing that feeling — celebrating with his teammates and pursuing a championship.
“I would much rather be here than being in Fort Myers and watching baseball,” he said. “I’ve learned in my second year now to not look too far ahead and just do everything I can to help the team win today.
“Just taking the field with these guys and getting to play with them every single day is a blast. It’s been great, and we’re to a point now in the year where you’re kind of right where you want to be as a squad.”

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
Roman Anthony couldn't put a ring on it. For more than two months, what had to have been one of the most annoying and nagging injuries kept Anthony out of the Boston Red Sox lineup. He had partially torn a ligament in his right ring finger. It wasn't some massive, noticeable, life-changing injury. It was just an ailment that made it really hard to swing a bat.
The Red Sox handled business in the meantime. They went on that franchise record-tying 15-game winning streak. They watched Ceddanne Rafaela become an All-Star. They saw Mickey Gasper temporarily turn into Ted Williams.
Then, in late August, Anthony came back. He was supposed to be the final piece to the puzzle. If the Red Sox were a good baseball team without Anthony, they could potentially be a great one with him -- at least, that's how the thinking went. The problem, though, is clear: Since Anthony has been back, he hasn't been quite right. He hasn't looked like a rising star. He's looked like a hitter who is recognizing that hitting is actually really, really hard.
There's not a whole lot of time for Anthony to right the ship before the postseason, but there's just enough time for Boston fans to hold out hope that he has (or will find) a solution.
If he's going to make fixes, it'll have to be in his approach at the plate, where he's whiffed at a 35% rate in September, including a stretch of 17 strikeouts in 35 plate appearances. Something clearly isn't quite right here, although it may not be as bad as you think.
Roman Anthony's Swing Looks Different When It Matters
One quick way to figure out what might be happening with a hitter who is striking out a lot is to fast forward directly to two-strike counts and see what's happening.
First, though, take a look at what Anthony looks like on the first pitch of an at-bat with two runners on base. This clip shows a wide stance that's slightly open, a strong leg kick, and Anthony's signature ability to stay through the baseball and drive it the other way:

Roman Anthony Since Returning From IL

AB: 61
R: 8
H: 16
HR: 3
RBI: 5
BB: 5
SO: 20
AVG: .262
OPS: .793 pic.twitter.com/zCDEPxL2xi

That's not the swing that Anthony has had lately on two strikes. If you want to be a sad Red Sox fan for a few minutes, this next video is for you (it shows Anthony's recent strikeout stretch). And if you watch closely, you'll see that not only is Anthony not setting up the same each time as on the hit in the video above. He's not even set up the same in all of these clips. Clearly, he's searching for a two-strike solution, but it's changing the openness of his stance, the height at which he stands, the level of his leg kick and even the apparent length of his swing:

Roman Anthony has struck out in 17 of his last 35 plate appearances, and his 2-strike approach has looked completely discombobulated. pic.twitter.com/r3q3tc5A64
— Stats (@redsoxstats) September 12, 2026
Some hitters change their approach with two strikes -- contact hitters in particular often get lower and choke up on the bat to have the best chance of putting the ball in play. But the big and strong Anthony, if he's going to do that, better at least stick to a plan. And it seems like right now he doesn't have one.
So we can see the video, and we can see the basic stats, but to further figure out what's been going wrong with Anthony, we decided to take a look at the metrics behind his swing itself.
Clearly, coming back from a finger injury and a long layoff could make hitting harder, but this isn't just about Anthony's .226 average and .677 OPS in September. The Red Sox need to figure out what's going on so they can address it and improve those numbers the rest of the way.
Lucky for us, Statcast has just about every metric you could possibly imagine, so it's possible to compare all sorts of things about Anthony's swing inputs and batted ball outputs from each month of his rookie season through right now.
Take, for example, his attack angle. That's the vertical direction the sweet spot is traveling when it hits the baseball. This month, Anthony has an attack angle of 16 degrees. When he had a .946 OPS in July of last year, it was 14 degrees. The only time it has ever been this high before was last September in a super small sample size (26 pitches seen). And while it may seem like a minor difference, it can prevent the ideal line drive from coming off Anthony's bat.
That's just one metric. The rest of his bat statistics actually seem fine. Nothing is weird about his bat speed or his swing length or his attack direction. There's nothing underlying there to be totally concerned about.
This is the part, Red Sox fans, where the news gets good.
Roman Anthony Is Actually Just Fine
Anthony's swing, while maybe a little tilted from its optimal self, doesn't seem broken. He's just whiffing a bit more than you'd want. It's also worth considering what happens when Anthony doesn't whiff.
When he's made contact the ball in September, Anthony has hit it harder than ever before. His previous best average exit velocity in a month was in July 2025, at 96.9 miles per hour.
Entering this week, Anthony has averaged 97.0 miles per hour of exit velocity on his batted balls in this month. He's had a hard-hit percentage of 63.6%, right about his career average, and he has the third-best single-month barrel rate of his career. The Red Sox obviously can't afford for him to keep whiffing on more than a third of the swings he takes, but we can also recognize that Anthony is oh so close to putting it back together again.

The limp to October goes on for the Boston Red Sox, who blew an early 2-0 lead Wednesday night, and dropped the series in Texas with a 7-3 loss that improved the Rangers to 76-76.
Boston batters managed just three hits, their runs coming via Willson Contreras’ first-inning two-run homer and Caleb Durbin scoring on a balk in the fifth.
Early on, it looked like both starting pitchers were not going to last long.
Rangers lefty MacKenzie Gore began Wednesday’s game with a four-pitch walk, three of which were nowhere near the zone, to Red Sox leadoff man Roman Anthony, and gave up Contreras’ team-leading 27th homer.
Sox rookie southpaw Jake Bennett labored through a 26-pitch bottom of the first in which he faced six batters and gave up a run.
But after a second-inning delay in which it seemed like Gore was about to depart, he completed four innings. Bennett went 4 2/3. Both starters allowed three earned runs, though Gore only yielded two hits to Bennett’s eight.
“Overall, not horrible,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters of Bennett. “The first inning they were able to make him throw some pitches, so the pitches stacked up on him. But at the end of the day, he left with the lead, was competitive. … Usually you’re accustomed to see him pitching deeper, but they were pesky with their at-bats, fouled a lot of stuff off, and drove the count up.”
The Red Sox retook the lead on Jakob Junis’ fifth-inning balk. It evaporated for good one pitch into Greg Weissert’s appearance when he took over for Bennett in the bottom of the inning.
Erik Miller’s three-run blowup seventh inning was the unnecessary coup de grâce for a Red Sox team struggling to so much as collect a hit, much less score a run. But it marked Miller’s worst outing of the season, with Boston or San Francisco, and his third time allowing runs in his last six appearances.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well, just not getting ahead of guys, falling behind counts, getting into hitters counts,” a subdued Miller told reporters postgame. “I mean, doesn’t really matter how good your stuff is; guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end as well.”
“Just kind of working through some stuff right now,” Miller continued. “There’s some stuff (I’m) trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. … At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. And I’d been doing really well, and some bad habits kind of fallen back into. So yeah, just got to work through it, kind of get back to what I was doing, and go from there.”
2018 World Series hero Nathan Eovaldi closed out the win with four shutout innings against his former team. It marked the veteran righty’s first relief appearance since 2020: Game 4 of the 2021 ALCS with the Red Sox.
To add insult to the injury of Boston’s decision not to re-sign Eovaldi following the 2022 season, his 46 wins since 2023 are tied for second-most among all American League pitchers in that span.
Trevor Story’s infield single in the fifth and Nick Sogard’s pinch-hit single in the sixth comprised the rest of Boston’s hits. The lineup managed three walks and struck out three times in the contest. They were 0 for 7 with runners in scoring position, and left three men on base.
“Yeah, we’re going through it a little bit,” Tracy said of his lineup. “We didn’t have a ton, we didn’t create a ton of opportunities.”
Game highlights were few and far between for the Red Sox. The short list included the usual elite defense from right fielder Wilyer Abreu, who is all but guaranteed to win his third consecutive Gold Glove Award, and continued displays of ABS expertise by new catcher Adley Rutschman, who went 3 for 3 in challenges.
The Red Sox have lost five of their last seven games since their five-game win streak. They are 7-7 in September, 10-11 in their last 20 games, and 82-70 overall.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason spot is five. But there is little magic lately.

The Boston Red are losers of four games out of their last six after dropping Tuesday's 4-2 decision to the Texas Rangers.
As they push to clinch a playoff spot, the Red Sox send rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69, 83 K) to the mound in the middle contest of the three game series in Texas.
Just hours before first pitch, the Red Sox announced a decision on their left-swinging outfielder Jarren Duran.
Duran is sitting out again Wednesday as the Boston Red Sox face Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore, extending a pattern now seven starts deep. The decision appears to be strictly a platoon move by interim manager Chad Tracy. There have been no reports that Duran is injured.
In fact, Boston has now benched its left-handed-hitting outfielder against every left-handed starter he has faced since Aug. 8, a stretch that raises concerns about how Duran fits into next season's outfield picture, and for the likely American League wild-card series matchup.
In that three-game series, the Red Sox appear certain to face at least one left-hander, possibly two, in Yankees starters Max Fried and Carlos Rodón.

Duran bats left-handed, Gore throws left-handed, and Boston's coaching staff has ceased to start Duran on days a southpaw takes the mound for the opponent.
Nate Eaton takes over in center field for Boston.
Texas had already turned in its own lineup behind Gore hours before first pitch, setting up the Wednesday matchup at Globe Life Field.
Duran's absence from the lineup against lefties has stretched to seven straight starts without facing a southpaw, dating back to his last look at left-handed pitching on Aug. 8, according to RotoWire. He sat again Sunday against Kansas City and was used only as a pinch-hitter, a role he has filled repeatedly this month.
There is no reported health issue behind Tracy's decision. Duran started Tuesday against right-hander Jacob deGrom, playing center field and batting seventh, and remains fully active on Boston's roster.
Duran is slashing .204/.261/.361 with 20 home runs across 141 games this season, and his OPS against left-handed pitching sits at .641, actually higher than his .616 mark against right-handers, according to FanGraphs. Boston has kept sitting him against lefties anyway.

Duran's Playing Time Has Dropped Sharply
Duran appeared in 160 games in 2024, when he led the American League in at-bats, doubles and triples, on his way to an All-Star selection and an eighth-place MVP finish. He followed that with 157 games in 2025.
This year he has played in 141 of Boston's games, a drop that traces to the growing run of benchings against left-handed hurlers. Wednesday marks at least the seventh time this season Boston has parked Duran for a left-handed starter, following earlier sit-downs against Rodón, Kyle Freeland, Jacob Lopez, Mitch Bratt and Reid Detmers, according to CBS Sports.
Boston opened the year with four outfielders competing for time, but an early injury to Roman Anthony briefly opened the picture before Duran struggled through a rough first half, batting .194 over his first 87 games. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out with a quad injury and Eli White is sidelined with a foot issue, leaving Eaton as the only regular right-handed option in center on days Duran sits.

Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

Since returning from injury on August 30, Roman Anthony has looked more like the 2025 version of himself than he did at the beginning of the season. He's hitting .258 with a .764 OPS. In his 15 games, he's got five RBI and six extra-base hits; it's good for a 109 WRC+. It's exactly what the Red Sox needed from him in his return from his May 4 injury.
The one thing Anthony has struggled with has been leading off the game. He has hit leadoff in every game he's played since his return and has only two singles, a double, and five strikeouts with no walks in that spot. It's probably time to have someone else lead off.
In his absence (May 5-August 29), Red Sox leadoff hitters had success in the first inning. While they only hit .213, they had a .307 on-base percentage and a .449 slugging percentage, which equated to a 108 WRC+. Surprisingly, most of that success came from Jarren Duran, who hit leadoff 31 of the 101 games and had a 141 WRC+.
Roman Anthony hasn't performed in the first inning, but he has the rest of the game
Anthony has struggled in the leadoff spot all season. In a total of 36 games, the lefty has a .299 OPS in the first inning. In the second inning or later this season, Anthony boasts a .280/.395/.439/.834 slash line and a 136 WRC+. In those same innings, in only the games he was first in the batting order, he has a .792 OPS and 125 WRC+.
Something about him batting first in the first inning isn't working for him. Whether it's his approach or the way pitchers are attacking him in that spot, Anthony hasn't been able to put it together this season. That's why it's time to drop him down in the order.
That doesn't mean to all of a sudden move him down to seventh in the order, but to push him down to second or third and put a player with high on-base skills in front of him. The Sox have had a few players show really great on-base skills this season. Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa are all players with an OBP over .340 this season. Having one of them leadoff, then getting on base in front of Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu would be extremely dangerous.
Anthony hasn't shown he can hack it leading off the game this season; it's been his one real weak point since his return. With two weeks until the start of the playoffs and a postseason berth almost assured (100% per FanGraphs as of September 15th), now is the time to experiment with the lineup and fix this problem before they get to October.

Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.

Ranger Suarez tossed his second straight seven-inning start and the Boston Red Sox scored in their final three at-bats en route to a 5-1 win over the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon.
Suarez (7-4) struck out eight, scattered five hits and allowed one run while completing his seven frames in 96 pitches as Boston (81-68) snapped its three-game losing streak.
Roman Anthony, Adley Rutschman and Nick Sogard each had multiple hits while Wilyer Abreu hit a two-run double that gave the Red Sox a sixth-inning lead they would not relinquish.
Carter Jensen’s 24th home run of the season marked the only scoring for Kansas City (66-83), which opened the series with a win Friday.
The Red Sox took the lead with two runs on three straight hits in the sixth. After Mickey Gasper and Rutschman knocked back-to-back singles to right to chase Royals starter Randy Dobnak (3-4), Abreu drove them home with a two-out double to deep center off reliever Anthony Gose.
The lead grew in each of the next two frames, beginning with Sogard hitting a leadoff double and scoring on Caleb Durbin’s RBI single off the Green Monster in the seventh.
After Garrett Whitlock struck out the side in the Royals’ eighth, Trevor Story and Sogard posted back-to-back doubles to plate another run.
Aroldis Chapman followed with a scoreless ninth to tab Suarez with the victory.
The teams plowed through three scoreless innings with just one baserunner: Bobby Witt Jr.’s one-out single in Kansas City’s opening frame. Suarez stranded him on third after recording back-to-back outs, including an inning-ending strikeout of Vinnie Pasquantino.
Suarez retired the Royals 1-2-3 on 10 pitches in the second and third innings while Dobnak faced the minimum, striking out three batters through the first third of the game.
In the fourth, Anthony turned a leadoff single through the right side into the opening run. After moving to second on Gasper’s grounder, Anthony scored when Rutschman knocked a single into center.
After finishing the fourth around Pasquantino’s two-out double, Suarez retired five straight before Jensen’s one-out solo homer inside Pesky’s Pole in the sixth. The southpaw stranded runners in the next two frames, including back-to-back strikeouts to cap the seventh.

BOSTON — In a one-run game against the Kansas City Royals’ last homestand, Boston Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story hit a one-out double off the wall, raced to second base and dove head-first into the bag.
He flipped over on his back and held onto the bag, a safe call upheld after a Royals’ challenge.
Advertisement
The Red Sox eventually lost that game, but it was a small play that represented the bigger picture: Story was back. A diving, flipping play would have been hard to imagine for Story — or anyone watching him — earlier this season as he battled through a sports hernia injury that left him hitting .206 with a .547 OPS after 41 games.
Following surgery in May and a rehab that forced him to miss 93 games this season, Story has made a quiet but impactful return to the team.
He has hit safely in 13 of 14 games since returning, including Tuesday’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Since his activation Aug. 30 in New York, Story has started at shortstop in 14 of the team’s 15 games, going 19-for-56 (.339) with seven doubles and six RBIs. He’s hoping to make up for lost time.
“That was, ideally, the point of the surgery, to get it and come back and be able to do the things that I know I can do,” the 33-year-old said.
“It’s not invisible,” he said of the sports hernia’s effects. “I don’t think you would expect it to be after surgery and coming back. But it’s so much better than it was, and I’m getting stronger. So I’m happy about that. And I’m happy with the way my body has reacted. I wanted to be a part of this.”
It’s admittedly a small sample size since Story has returned, but if he had started slowly following his return, the calls for him to be replaced in the lineup would have grown louder. His replacements at shortstop — particularly a combination of Andruw Monasterio and Nick Sogard — filled in admirably during his absence as the Red Sox turned their season around. Story’s unproductive 10 rehab games with Triple-A Worcester, coupled with the rise of top prospect Franklin Arias, a shortstop raking at Triple A, created an echo chamber of angst about Story returning and underperforming.
So far, he hasn’t.
Advertisement
And he’s heard much of the criticism and frustration about his impending return. He understands it. His injury-riddled tenure in Boston has warranted that consternation. He missed much of 2024 recovering from extensive shoulder surgery and 2023 from elbow surgery. Of his five years in Boston, on a six-year, $140 million deal, he’s played only one healthy season.
Staying on the field has been his biggest bugaboo with the Red Sox. But the outside noise and frustration with his injuries motivated Story to prove he can still play.
“You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.”
Roman Anthony, who missed 101 games with a torn finger ligament and rehabbed alongside Story, learned by watching the veteran handle the pressure.
“He’s unbelievable,” said Anthony. “Getting to go through this process with him. I was so happy for him. Every at-bat, he just continues to look better and better, and then to trust himself through all the noise.”
The return to the field has taken Story some effort, though. He arrives at the field roughly an hour before the team’s mandatory report time so that he can get on the trainer’s table to be stretched out for 30 to 45 minutes before his activation work in the gym, which leads into the team’s daily hitters’ meeting, then his workout before cage and field work.
“I’ve learned to kind of streamline it a little bit, and with the injury, (I) kind of know what (I) need,” he said. “In the gym, I’m just activating the right muscles, getting the core going, getting the hips right, adductor, glute med, the surrounding muscles from my surgery. So a lot of it is pre-hab. It’s mainly about the hips and getting the rotations right.”

The work has paid off early on. On Aug. 31, his first game back at Fenway Park in nearly four months, he cranked a base hit off the wall in the bottom of the ninth for a walk-off win.
This past Sunday, he padded a slim Red Sox lead against the Royals with a two-run single in the eighth. He’s hoping to carry this production through the rest of the season to prove he can be the player who hit .289 with an .827 OPS over the final four months of the 2025 season.
Despite missing so much of the year, the recent production since has helped him feel a part of the Red Sox’ run.
“As I’m sitting there watching the 15-game winning streak and starting to turn the whole season around, you watch it from the dugout and it’s like, ‘Man, this is something special,'” he said. “To be able to play a part and do my thing this late in the season means a lot to me.”

Red Sox Video
The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. With just over 10 games left in the season, it’d take a whole mess of crazy for the Sox to move up or down. While it would be great to have a shot at moving up in the standings, their current situation will allow them to spend the final two weeks of the season freshening up their stalwarts, getting injury returnees back up to speed, and fixing Jarren Duran.
Duran hasn’t quite been the worst regular in Major League Baseball, but that’s damning with faint praise. He’s still an excellent baserunner and a plus fielder, but only Ezequiel Tovar has a lower wRC+ (51) among qualified hitters than Duran’s mark of 67. Despite his disintegrated noodle of a bat, he has racked up 578 plate appearances due to injuries and, presumably, a lack of better options, but that doesn’t make him a lost cause.
What makes Duran’s complete collapse at the plate so shocking is that he was a top-25 hitter by wRC+ only two seasons ago (132), and well above average just last season (112). While it’s safe to assume 2024 was a career year, he looked to have established himself as an above-average bat, and it’s not like all of his underlying metrics have cratered. If anything, many have improved.
He’s swinging the bat as fast as ever. His barrel rate is almost identical to the past two seasons. He’s pulling the ball in the air more. And while his in-zone contact rate is a career-low 84%, that’s a completely fair trade-off for what should be better power.
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
Now, you could argue that Duran didn’t need to change his approach from 2024, but given these figures, there’d be no reason to believe he had gone from one of the best hitters in baseball to almost the very worst. However, this chart doesn’t contain every last kernel of underlying data, and the one thing that has cratered for Duran is the most basic, fundamental skill of hitting—not chasing (f***ing) fastballs out of the zone.
Duran is running a wRC+ of 67 because his out-of-zone swing rate (O-Swing%) has ballooned to 34.5%, which is largely driven by a career-high O-Swing% of 36.8% against four-seam fastballs. Throughout his career, Duran’s production has largely followed his ability to lay off pitches out of the zone, but his inability to lay off four-seam fastballs (FA), to this degree, is new.
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
What makes his cratering performance against four-seamers so baffling is that it is exclusively down to swing decisions. His production when he makes contact is relatively unchanged, and he’s not whiffing a concerning amount in the zone. In fact, his zone contact rate against four-seamers is better than it was in 2024.
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
It’s not groundbreaking analysis to say that swinging at fastballs out of the zone is a bad idea, but it doesn’t necessarily doom a hitter to the abyss. However, Duran’s ability against four-seamers was a load-bearing trait, and it becoming a weakness has completely collapsed his profile because it has cost him the platoon advantage.
Unsurprisingly, Duran, a left-handed hitter, has made a career out of pulverizing right-handed pitching. His career wRC+ against righties is 114, compared to 72 against lefties. Splits like this are far from unusual, but what has happened to Duran in 2026 is. Over 410 plate appearances against righties, he has a wRC+ of 63. That’s the second-worst among qualified hitters, and it all stems from his struggles against four-seam fastballs.
This season, 37.3% of the pitches right-handers have thrown Duran have been four-seam fastballs, right in line with his career average of 38.7%. While four-seamers generally have more neutral platoon splits, historically, Duran absolutely feasted on right-handed four-seamers. Entering 2026, Duran had a +20.6 run value against right-handed four-seam fastballs, but he has somehow managed an absolutely preposterous, incomprehensible -13.1 run value in 2026.
The reason why Duran’s plate discipline has completely collapsed against four-seamers is a bit more of a mystery, but I think it starts with his increased desire to swing hard, lift, and pull. Over the past four seasons, as Duran’s swing speed has increased, he has hit the ball out in front a bit more.
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
None of this is particularly surprising and should be expected. A faster bat will make contact out in front more often, and bat speed increases throughout a swing. The two moving in tandem make all the sense in the world, but getting to this point could have come at a cost.
To sell out for swing speed and contact out in front, Duran likely has to get his operation started just a fraction of a second earlier, which means committing to pitches a tad earlier as well. The trickle-down effect is swinging at more pitches out of the zone, and in particular four-seam fastballs, which require the quickest decisions at the plate.
The Red Sox don’t need Jarren Duran to figure it out to make the playoffs, but getting him back to basics could unlock another level of the offense. With Duran producing at an average offensive level, suddenly the Sox could field an elite outfield defense of Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Duran, while letting Roman Anthony DH. However, for that dream arrangement to work, Duran needs to actually hit again, and that starts with laying off fastballs outside of the zone.

ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”

Boston Red Sox fans will not be seeing former top prospect Kristian Campbell in the big leagues at all this season, unfortunately.
On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that Campbell's season is over. Campbell was placed on the seven-day Injured List due to a left foot contusion on Sep. 10. Cassell reported that Campbell will not be able to return before Triple-A Worcester's season ends on Sep. 20.
"Some injury updates today in AAA Worcester: Tanner Houck is scheduled to pitch one inning (20-25 pitches) in relief," Cassell wrote. "Romy Gonzalez is in at DH despite being a bit banged up. Iggy Suarez mentioned he's "an option" to contribute with the Red Sox moving forward. Kristian Campbell is out for the rest of the WooSox season. 'He was a big part of what we've been doing,' Suarez said. 'So, it's definitely a downer for that.'"
Kristian Campbell Is Done For The Year
That's some really unfortunate news for one of the most intriguing players in the Red Sox's system. Campbell made the big league club out of Spring Training in 2025 as the first member of the "Big 3," including him, Roman Anthony and Marcelo Mayer. He was red-hot out of the gate to the point that Boston handed him an eight-year, $60 million deal. But things took a turn afterward. Campbell was demoted to Triple-A in June, 2025. He hasn't been in the majors since.
Campbell played in 73 down in Triple-A last season and then didn't make the Red Sox's big league club out of camp. He has been down in the minors all season this year trying to work his way back.
The 24-year-old spent the season in the outfield as Boston tried to slow things down after moving him around all over the place last year. For Boston, it is loaded in the outfield to the point that there was a logjam early on in the season. Then, despite the Red Sox losing Roman Anthony to the Injured List for a while, there still wasn't space for Campbell in the majors.
Overall, Campbell wrapped up his season after playing in 109 games for Triple-A and slashing .256/.383/.380 with a .763 OPS, eight homers and 51 RBIs. Hopefully, he's able to get back on track and get back into the mix by the time Spring Training rolls around. Who could've seen this coming back in 2025? Campbell looked like a franchise cornerstone piece. Unfortunately, he hasn't been in the majors in over a year and now that won't be happening this year.

BOSTON (WHDH) - Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle Sunday became just the sixth pitcher in MLB history to throw an immaculate inning in the first inning of a game. An immaculate inning occurs when a pitcher records three strikeouts on nine pitches.
The 23-year-old lefty has quickly become a fan favorite through not only his pitching prowess, but by showcasing his infectious personality. On the eighth pitch of the inning, Tolle flashed a bright smile into the Red Sox dugout before getting Kansas City Royals right fielder Jac Caglianone to strikeout swinging, completing the rare feat.
“We saw him smile towards the end and…said ‘oh my gosh it’s almost immaculate inning,’ and then he got it. And we were just floored,” said Caroline Stacey, a Red Sox fan from Maine. “Tolle is such a great player, he’s so fun to watch. Like, everything he does is just fun so it was really great to see him celebrate and have such an amazing accomplishment.”
The last Red Sox player to throw an immaculate inning at the start of a game was Hall-of-Famer Pedro Martinez in 2002. The then-30-year-old struck out three Mariners in a row on May 18.
“Unbelievable. Eighth in the history of the Red Sox is, I mean, unbelievable,” said Chris Molina, a Red Sox fan visiting Boston from Kansas.
After the game, Tolle said he hopes to ignite the team in any way he can.
“Trying to be the spark in whatever way I can. If that’s pitching or that’s offense, just trying to find that way is kind of what I want to do,” he explained.
It’s that spark that has him winning over the city of Boston as well as his teammates. Red Sox star outfielder Roman Anthony praised Tolle during an on field interview after the game on NESN.
“You see the amount of people that are behind him, and the energy he brings to Red Sox baseball and the city of Boston,” Anthony said. “Everyone around, they ride for him, and we feel that energy when he’s on the bump the minute he takes it. He’s such an amazing person, and an amazing teammate who’s there for us every single day, and whether he’s pitching or not he brings that energy. So it’s so fun to be behind him. He’s amazing.”
The manager of the Red Sox Team Store says they can barely keep his jersey stocked on the shelves as the demand has become so high.
“When you combine the talent that he has with the personality that he has – we’ve seen this before with certain guys like Johnny Damon, David Ortiz, who were big personalities and great players – I mean, that means he’s going to be a star for years to come,” said Tim Pettit, Manager of the Red Sox Team Store.
Following the immaculate inning, Tolle went on to throw five more scoreless innings, finishing with seven strikeouts. The Red Sox went on to beat the Royals 4-1 and secure the series win.
